Hi Sam / Priya,

Thanks again for the call earlier. Per our discussion, I wanted to capture a short primer on the three connectivity patterns we see most often for Redwood Private deployments: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (VPC endpoints), and Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec).

We've seen customers choose each option depending on:
- control-plane isolation requirements (can Redwood reach your VPC directly?)
- CIDR overlap constraints
- expected throughput and latency SLAs
- operational ownership (your network team vs. our managed endpoints)

Hi Sam / Lauren,

I pulled together practical pros/cons and operational notes below — short and focused on AWS since that’s the stack you referenced. Happy to expand to Azure/GCP if needed.

1) VPC Peering - Pros:
  - L3 routing between VPCs, low latency, full L3 visibility (good for high-throughput workloads).
  - Simple, no additional proxying.
- Cons:
  - Transitive routing not supported (peering is point-to-point) — for multi-VPC setups you need Transit Gateway (adds cost/complexity).
  - CIDR overlap prevents peering; requires address planning or NAT to resolve.
  - Exposes pinned routes into your routing tables; if you prefer strict isolation, peering gives broader access unless tightly controlled by NACLs/security groups.
- Operational notes:
  - Use AWS Resource Access Manager + cross-account roles for automated peering creation.
  - Ensure MTU (jumbo frames) parity and TCP MSS clamping if your on-prem equipment manipulates MTU.

2) AWS PrivateLink (Interface VPC Endpoints / Endpoint Services) - Pros:
  - Endpoint-based connectivity — we create an endpoint service in our VPC and you create an interface endpoint in yours.
  - Avoids CIDR overlap issues because traffic is routed to ENIs, not via VPC route tables.
  - Better security posture: only the published service ports are exposed, and access can be controlled via endpoint policies.
  - No transitive routing concerns; cleaner per-service isolation.
- Cons:
  - Slightly higher per-GB cost (endpoint hours + data processing).
  - Some protocols may require TCP-only; less suitable for non-TCP patterns.
  - Latency: typically a single-digit ms overhead at p95 inside the same region; cross-account+AZ would usually keep <10ms p95 but depends on AZ pairing and ENI placement. Test required for strict <30ms SLOs.
- Operational notes:
  - Use Private DNS names to ensure clients hit the endpoint.
  - We recommend enabling endpoint health checks and using multiple AZ endpoints for HA.

3) Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec) - Pros:
  - Works with on-prem equipment, supports dynamic routing (BGP) for easier prefix management.
  - Good when you cannot or will not route cloud traffic directly into your VPCs.
  - Encryption termination on your edge — aligns with some compliance requirements.
- Cons:
  - Higher and variable latency vs native cloud connectivity; depends on ISP transit.
  - Throughput depends on both on-prem hardware and cloud VPN concentrator limits (AWS VGW has throughput tiers; use AWS Transit Gateway + VPN attachments for scale).
  - Long-term operational burden: ops must manage tunnels, rekeying, and failover.
- Operational notes:
  - Recommend BGP with ASNs and advertise only required subnets.
  - Use redundant tunnels across two VGWs or Transit Gateway for HA.
  - If you need stable high throughput, consider Direct Connect or Partner Interconnect instead of VPN for production-critical low-latency workloads.

Recommendations summary:
- If you need low-latency, high-throughput intra-cloud connectivity and no CIDR overlap: VPC peering (or Transit Gateway for multi-VPC) is simplest.
- If CIDR overlap or strict per-service exposure is required: PrivateLink is safer and cleaner.
- For on-prem to cloud connectivity or when egress must remain on-prem: S2S VPN (or Direct Connect) is the right pattern.

Hi team,

Adding a short recommendation checklist and a pragmatic design we often use with enterprise customers that balances performance and isolation:

Recommended hybrid pattern (works well for Acme use-case):
- Control plane & management traffic: PrivateLink to your management VPC
  - Why: minimal blast radius, works around CIDR overlap, and we can gate service access with endpoint policies.
- Data plane / heavy traffic (if low-latency required): Transit Gateway + VPC peering for our data VPCs, or Direct Connect if you already have it.
  - Why: avoids VPN throughput variability and keeps p95 low.
- On-Prem connectivity: terminate redundant IPsec tunnels into Transit Gateway (BGP) for route propagation and HA.

Checklist for Acme network team to provide before the design call:
- VPC CIDRs for all candidate VPCs (management, data, shared services).
- Public egress IPs and allowed destination ports for firewall rules (we need to know which IPs our endpoints will use).
- Preferred ASN and whether you want BGP or static routing for VPN.
- Any PKI/mTLS requirements for control-plane APIs.
- Expected sustained throughput to Redwood (GB/day, peak Mbps).

Small config notes:
- PrivateLink: create one interface endpoint per AZ for HA, use endpoint policies to limit to specific service principals, and enable Private DNS to preserve hostnames.
- VPN: PSK+pre-shared key can be used for initial testing but recommend certificate-based IPsec for production where your appliance supports it.
- Routing: prefer BGP for dynamic failover; advertise only specific subnets.

I've attached vpn-config-template.txt and will post a pre-reqs spreadsheet to the drive (see link). Happy to run through the checklist on the call.

— Dev
